node.label: Life Lived Like a Story (Sidney, Smith, Ned and Cruikshank, 1990)
node.date_label: Family request 1974 · UBC Press and Nebraska 1990 · paperback 1992 · reviewed 1992 · cited as a model 2009–10
node.description: A book credited to Julie Cruikshank 'in collaboration with' three Yukon elders, Angela Sidney, Kitty Smith and Annie Ned, who told their life stories; Cruikshank recorded and arranged them. The project began in 1974, when 'younger members of their respective families … asked Cruikshank to record their autobiographies' (McClellan 1992). The narrators chose the form: Sidney and Smith wove personal incidents with 'well-known stories from the traditional narrative repertoire', and Ned 'chose to emphasize songs and oratory'. Cruikshank, Gmelch wrote, 'gradually shifted her research focus from documenting their lives … to examining the actual way they talked about, remembered, and interpreted their lives'. Reviewers called it 'a work of true collaboration between native and non-native' and 'a valuable model of how collaboration between an anthropologist or oral historian and their native teachers can work'; McClellan also noted that Cruikshank 'selected the material' and 'arranged it'.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Angela Sidney, Kitty Smith, Annie Ned and Julie Cruikshank, Life Lived Like a Story: Life Stories of Three Yukon Native Elders (Vancouver: UBC Press; Lincoln: University of Nebraska Press, 1990; Bison paperback 1992). Readers: Catharine McClellan (Arctic, 1992); Sharon Gmelch (BC Studies, 1992); Carlson, Lutz and Schaepe (2009); Leddy (2010).
node.scope_note: A packaged collaborative entry (user decision, 2026-10-27): the four are credited together as the book credits them ('in collaboration with'), not as a Cruikshank person entry. The book itself is unread (no allowed open text). The entry rests on the publisher description and two contemporary reviews read in full (McClellan, Arctic 45:2, 1992, 205–206; Gmelch, BC Studies 94, 1992, 85–86); Cruikshank's words are given only 'as quoted by' them. Under the OCAP limits (2026-10-27) the entry describes the collaboration's method and authorship only: no narratives, songs or words of the narrators are quoted, and the narrators are named as the book credits them. Later uses read in Carlson, Lutz and Schaepe (2009) and Leddy (2010). Cruikshank's later books are separate.

proposed_edges.relationship: Three Yukon elders and an anthropologist made life histories at the families' request in forms the narrators chose; reviewers called it 'a work of true collaboration', and historians later cite the four as their precedent.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: McClellan 1992 pp. 205–206 (1974 family request; narrators' forms; 'a work of true collaboration between native and non-native'); Gmelch 1992 p. 86 ('a valuable model of how collaboration … can work'); cited with all four names by Carlson, Lutz and Schaepe 2009 (p. 2 n. 4) and Leddy 2010 (p. 2 n. 5). Cruikshank's selection and ordering (McClellan p. 205) is kept. Book unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Shifts the oral historian's question from documenting lives to 'the actual way they talked about, remembered, and interpreted their lives', and shows the limits of the Western life-history form.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Gmelch 1992 pp. 85–86 (her own words: the shift of focus; 'a cautionary reminder of the limitations of the conventional life history or autobiographical form'). McClellan quotes Cruikshank that 'autobiography is a culturally specific narrative genre' (p. x) and oral tradition is 'a window on the ways in which the past is culturally constituted and discussed' (p. 14), as quoted by McClellan p. 205. Replaces the Yukon part of edge_125.

proposed_edges.relationship: Reviewed as 'a sophisticated and ground-breaking contribution to anthropological scholarship and practice' that points to a new relationship between Native peoples and anthropologists.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: McClellan 1992 p. 206: 'Embodying mutual respect and understanding, this book points to the kind of relationship between native Americans and anthropologists that both groups can increasingly hope for'. edge_042 (anthropology → indigenous) stays for Buck, Smith and Wilson.
